learningObjective: Distinguish Hillis-Steele (work-inefficient) from Blelloch (work-efficient) parallel prefix scan.

canonicalClaims.claim: Hillis-Steele scan has depth O(log N) with O(N log N) work; Blelloch scan has depth O(log N) with O(N) work. Blelloch is work-efficient but requires more complex indexing (up-sweep + down-sweep) and typically needs SMEM padding to avoid bank conflicts.
conditions: N is a power of two; shared memory used.
nonImplications: Does not imply Blelloch is always faster in practice on GPUs.
Does not imply either algorithm handles non-associativity.

misconceptions.claim: Hillis-Steele and Blelloch have identical work.
misconceptions.whyWrong: O(N log N) vs O(N) is a real complexity difference.

misconceptions.claim: Hillis-Steele requires commutativity; Blelloch does not.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Both require associativity; commutativity is not the differentiator.
Depth is O(log N) — that is the point of the balanced tree.

misconceptions.claim: Blelloch has no bank-conflict issues on shared memory.
misconceptions.whyWrong: The non-uniform stride pattern commonly hits bank conflicts; padding is a standard mitigation.

implementationFacts: Common padding trick: index by `idx + idx/NUM_BANKS`.
performanceScenarios: For small N (e.g., a single warp), Hillis-Steele's simplicity often wins; for larger blocks, Blelloch's lower work wins.
